subject: sociology
title: Beliefs & Secularisation: Critiques & Believing Without Belonging
welcome_lead: Religion changes, doesn't simply die — Davie and Heelas push back.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology secularisation critiques Davie Heelas spiritual revolution.
final_note: Decline of churches isn't decline of belief.

concepts.def: Davie — minority practise on behalf of majority.
Heelas & Woodhead — turn from traditional to New Age.
Stark & Bainbridge — religion thrives where there is choice.
Norris & Inglehart — religion fades where life feels secure.

walkthroughs.body_html: Davie (1994): most Britons still believe in something supernatural; only practice declines. 2001 census 72% Christian despite ~5% attendance. Vicarious religion: clergy and regular attenders do religion on behalf of a sympathetic majority — used at Diana's funeral.

Heelas & Woodhead (2005) studied the small town of Kendal. Congregational sector (church) had been larger but was declining; holistic milieu (yoga, reiki) was growing. Argued for a spiritual revolution — not secularisation but transformation.

Stark & Bainbridge (1985): US has high religiosity because of religious market — pluralism stimulates participation. Norris & Inglehart (2004): religion declines where existential security is high — secularisation matches GDP, not modernity per se.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between reliability and validity in research?
options: Religion is becoming more important globally.
Reliable research is published in journals; valid research isn't.
Reliable and valid mean the same thing — that the research is good.
Reliability is whether a method produces consistent results when repeated; validity is whether it actually measures what it claims to. A method can be reliable but invalid, or valid but unreliable.
